newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault woes revive Europe car merger talks. [CORRECTED 16:43 GMT, 22/03]
newsitem.headline: Renault woes revive Europe car merger talks. [CORRECTED 16:43 GMT, 22/03]

text.p: Renault SA's plunge into huge losses has revived talk in France of car company mergers after a long silence following the collapse three years ago of an alliance between Renault and Sweden's Volvo.
(Corrects number of years from two).
Prime Minister Alain Juppe has said the government was looking at whether mergers were needed before liberalisation of the European market in the year 2000.

"We need to look at what groupings between French or European companies now appear essential because at the end of this century, in two or three years, cars from outside the European Community, from Japan and Korea, will come in freely," Juppe said.
"If we're not ready to handle the shock, the whole industry would be vulnerable," he said on Thursday.
Juppe was speaking after Renault reported a 5.25 billion franc ($920.4 million) loss for 1996, including 3.91 billion francs in charges to cut nearly 6,000 jobs this year in France and Belgium.
Renault and its domestic rival PSA Peugeot Citroen are hampered by their small size and dependence on the slow-growing European market which is set to become the global battleground in the year 2000.

The Peugeot group is in better shape than Renault, which entered the private sector less than a year ago. But analysts estimate its profit fell 30 percent in 1996 after a 45 percent drop in the preceding year.

Former French president Valery Giscard-d'Estaing recommended a merger of the two companies. "Such an alliance, while difficult, would not be insurmountable," he said in a commentary in the magazine L'Express.

A merger would create the biggest European car company, overtaking Volkswagen, and the fifth largest worldwide. "If this project were carried out, it would be a great day for the future of the French auto industry," he said.
A question has hung over the fate of the two carmakers, Renault in particular, since the rejection by Volvo's shareholders of an alliance with then state-owned Renault.
Car analysts say the collapse highlighted the difficulties involved in merging car companies which, like airlines, are considered flag-carriers.
The French shudder at the fate of Britain's car industry, which has turned into subsidiaries of such giants as Ford, General Motors Corp and BMW.

Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer speaks with regret of the collapsed deal which left Renault struggling as the smallest of the six companies producing a full range of cars in Europe. It is unlikely now to end up as the dominant partner in a merger.

He said recently that a merger with the Peugeot group was not the answer. "If the two groups were brought together...the French industry would be the first casualty because we'd see sales volumes and market share collapse," Schweitzer said.
But he said he agreed with Industry Minister Franck Borotra's proposals for greater cooperation among the two on joint projects, such as their V6 engine venture.

Peugeot's outspoken chairman Jacques Calvet was characteristically more blunt. "A merger with another carmaker? Never, never, never and definitely not with another French carmaker," he said at the Geneva car show this month.

Some analysts say an all-French merger would be difficult because the two companies have too much overlapping business. They say Fiat, which is struggling much like the French to become a global player after acquiring Lancia and Alfa-Romeo, may be a good match for one of the French companies.
Mercedes-Benz's truck and luxury car businesses would also complement companies specialising in small cars.
But analysts say mergers would not prevent job losses in the European car industry. If anything, they would accelerate staff reduction as companies trimmed overlapping operations.

"At the end of the day, it would make eminent sense for Peugeot or Renault to merge, or Peugeot with Fiat," said one analyst. "The question is, how prepared are governments to follow that logic through, with the losses of tens of thousands of jobs?" ($ = 5.704 French Francs)
